## How the test suite is organised and run (`ctest`) {#sec-ch13-suite}

### Summary

kintera has two kinds of tests: C++ programs written with GoogleTest, and Python test files run by `pytest`. CMake
registers both with `ctest`, so one `ctest` command in the build's test directory runs everything. A C++ test that
takes a device runs on CPU and CUDA, in single and double precision. Its CUDA instances skip when no GPU is
available.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** One `ctest` run covers the C++ and the Python tests.

**Data.** 49 `ctest` entries at the pin: 16 C++ programs, one grouped Python entry and 32 single-file Python entries.

**Placement.** After the build: `ctest` in `build/tests`.

**Activation.** Always registered; a C++ file is built only if `tests/CMakeLists.txt` names it.

**Guarantee / limits.** Seven C++ test files in the tree are not built (Limits).

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

### Derivation

No derivation: this scheme is the organisation of the tests.

### Numerical method

No numerical method. The registration in {{< code tests/CMakeLists.txt >}} works in three steps:

1. Each C++ test named by the `setup_test` macro ({{< code cmake/macros/macro_setup_test.cmake >}}) becomes one
   executable `<name>.release`, linked with GoogleTest's `main` and, in a CUDA build, with the CUDA library. It is
   registered as one `ctest` entry of the same name.
2. Eight Python files whose native calls already run in child processes are run together by one entry,
   `test_python_subprocess`, so they share one `pytest` start-up.
3. Every other `tests/test*.py` file becomes its own entry, named after the file, which runs `pytest <file>` from
   the source directory.

The C++ tests that take a device derive from `DeviceTest` ({{< code tests/device_testing.hpp DeviceTest >}}). The
default instantiation runs each such test four times: CPU and CUDA, each in single and double precision. The fixture
skips the CUDA instances when `torch::cuda::is_available()` is false.

TODO: a figure of the registration (source files to executables and `ctest` entries).

**Running the tests and reading the counts.** In the build's test directory, `ctest -N` lists the registered
entries without running them, `ctest --output-on-failure` runs them all, and `ctest -R <regex>` runs those whose
names match; the exact entry names are in Appendix C (@sec-appc). A Python file can also be run directly from the
source tree with `python -m pytest tests/<file> -rs`, which prints the reason of every skipped case. Four things
decide what a run means:

1. **What was built.** CUDA cases need a `-DCUDA=ON` build (@sec-ch12-build); a C++ file that `tests/CMakeLists.txt`
   does not name is never built (Limits).
2. **What the entry can start.** The single-file Python entries call `pytest` by name. When `pytest` is not on the
   `PATH`, `ctest` reports those entries as `Not Run` and counts them as failures, while the C++ entries still pass.
3. **What the inputs are.** The C++ tests read the input files linked into `build/tests` (Limits); some Python cases
   need external data files and skip without them (@sec-ch13-results).
4. **What a pass hides.** One `ctest` entry is a whole file. It passes when every case passes or skips, so a passing
   entry can contain skipped cases. On a CPU build, `test_reaction_equilibrium.py` is one passing entry, while
   `pytest` reports 63 of its 120 cases passed and 57 skipped because no CUDA device is present. A file whose module
   skips as a whole is counted by `ctest` as a failure.

Listing an entry is not running it, and running a file is not running every case in it.[^ch13-suite-run]

**Which tests verify conservation in the equilibrium solvers.** Being registered does not make a test a verification
of conservation; this map gives, for the two equilibrium solvers, which test asserts which conserved quantity, to
what tolerance, and what it leaves open. The NASA-9 case is `test_nasa9_yaml_equilibrium_case`, the ideal-gas case
the gtest `IdealGasReaction`:

| test (solver) | quantity | assertion | tolerance | what it does not establish |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `test_saturation_adjustment_nh4sh.py` (fixed $U$, $V$, @sec-ch04-equilibrate-uv) | N and S atoms of 2000 random cells | element sums before and after | `rtol=1e-12`, `atol=0` | energy; the fixed-$T$ solver |
| `test_reaction_equilibrium.py` (fixed $T$, $p$ and $U$, $V$; 13 reactions, 8 cases each) | amounts along the reaction, $n - n_0 - \nu\,\xi$ | against an independent extent solve | $2\times10^{-6}$ (double), $2\times10^{-3}$ (single), relative | energy: its energy error is recomputed at the temperature read back from $U$, so it holds by construction |
| `test_equilibrium.py`, NASA-9 case (log-K solver, @sec-ch05-conditions) | H and O atoms of one gas cell at 4000 K | element sums before and after | `assert_close` defaults for double, `rtol=1e-7`, `atol=1e-7` | several phases |
| `test_equilibrium.release`, ideal-gas case (log-K solver) | total amount of A $\rightleftharpoons$ B | sum equals 1 | `rtol=1e-6`, `atol=1e-6` | element balance of other reactions |

: Conservation tests of the equilibrium solvers. {#tbl-ch13-suite-conservation}

Not verified by any test at the pin: conservation of the internal energy by the fixed-$U$, $V$ solver beyond
construction (@sec-ch04-equilibrate-uv proposes a saturation check at the host temperature instead); element
conservation of the log-K solver with several phases (@sec-ch05-newton measures it outside the suite); and the
status codes 1 to 4 of the log-K solver (@sec-ch05-diagnostics).

**Validation tolerances.** In this report, a validation tolerance is the largest difference a test accepts between a
computed value and its reference, as an absolute bound, a relative bound or both. It is not the stopping tolerance
of a solver, such as `ftol`, which decides when an iteration ends. A validation tolerance must allow for that
stopping tolerance and for everything else between the computed value and the reference: the floating-point
precision and the number of operations, the discretization error when the reference is an exact solution, and the
uncertainty of the reference itself. A tolerance chosen this way is a bound with a reason; one written into a test
without a reason only records what passed once.

Worked example, `IdealGasReaction`: A $\rightleftharpoons$ B with $\ln K^\circ = 0$ and `ftol` $10^{-7}$. The solver
stops when $|\ln(x_B/x_A)| \le \max(\ln(1+10^{-7}), 4\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}})$ (@sec-ch05-diagnostics). With
$x_A = 1/(1 + e^{r})$, a residual $r$ moves $x_A$ from 0.5 by about $|r|/4$, so the derived bound on
$|x_A - 0.5|$ is $2.5\times10^{-8}$ in double and $1.8\times10^{-7}$ in single precision, rounding of $x_A$
included. The test allows $10^{-6} + 10^{-5}\times 0.5 = 6\times10^{-6}$. The measured differences are
$5.6\times10^{-9}$ and $6.0\times10^{-8}$.[^ch13-suite-tol] The test's bound is consistent with the derivation, about
30 times the single-precision bound, but the test states no reason for it, as is the case for most tolerances of the
suite (the "where the tolerance comes from" columns of chapters 4, 5 and 12). A test passing within such a bound
shows agreement to that bound, not that the bound is the accuracy of the code.

: Code map of the test suite. {#tbl-ch13-suite-code}

At configure time, `tests/CMakeLists.txt` links every `*.inp`, `*.dat` and `*.yaml` file of `tests/` into
`build/tests` with `ln -sf`, because the C++ tests read their inputs from there.

files and 40 Python test files: 16 C++ programs are built, 8 Python files run in the grouped entry and 32 run as
single-file entries.

### Limits

- **Seven C++ test files are not built.** `tests/CMakeLists.txt` names no target for `test_ammonium_hydrosulfide.cpp`,
  `test_convective_adjustment.cpp`, `test_earth_thermo.cpp`, `test_jup_thermo.cpp`, `test_moist_adiabat.cpp`,
  `test_kinetics_rates.cpp` or `test_yaml_parse.cpp`. The last two appear only in commented-out lines. Their
  assertions do not run.
- **Inputs are linked, not copied.** On a file system that refuses symbolic links, the inputs are absent from
  `build/tests`, and the C++ tests that read them are expected to fail on a missing file. That failure was not
  measured at the pin: the runs of @sec-ch13-results copied the inputs by hand first.
